Selected work

Case studies

Case study 01
Integra SCADA HMI Redesign
UGL · UX Designer, Design Team · Desktop + Mobile · 2022-2025
Safety-criticalInfrastructureDesktop + Mobile
Opening

When an infrastructure operator misses a critical alarm, the consequences are not just a poor user experience; they can become a service failure or safety risk. My focus was to redesign the alarm experience around one practical question: what does an operator need to stay in control under pressure?

The problem

Operators worked in 24/7 control rooms with a legacy interface causing visual inconsistency, unreliable alarm hierarchy, and eye strain across long shifts. We observed operators scanning through dozens of simultaneous alarms, unable to quickly identify which required immediate action.

"When something goes wrong, everything goes red. I can't tell what's actually on fire."

, Operator, contextual inquiry
Key design decisions
01. Dark theme, sustained attention not preference

Operators work in low-ambient control rooms across 8 to 12 hour shifts. A dark theme was an environmental decision, validated against WCAG 2.1 AA. Consistency across all operators matters more than personal preference in a safety-critical environment.

02. Three-tier alarm prioritisation

Restructured alarms around Critical, Elevated, and Informational, using visual weight rather than colour alone. Critical alarms occupy a persistent top zone. Priority-first matched how operators think in an emergency.

03. Modular components, consistency as a safety feature

A shared Figma component library with strict behavioural rules. Any component responds identically across every screen. Consistency here is not a design preference; it is a safety consideration.

Outcomes
Priority
Alarm hierarchy clarified
WCAG AA
Accessibility considered
1 library
Reusable UI system
Reflection

Involve operators earlier. I would have fought harder for that access from day one. Good design in complex environments is as much about what you remove as what you add.

Case study 02
Performance Management System, Transport for NSW
UGL · Sole UX Designer · Web + Mobile · 2023-2025
Government0→1 ProductCross-platformEnterprise
Opening

Managing Sydney's train fleet involved maintenance, operations and payment-reporting workflows that needed to work together. I was the sole designer on this project and led the UX design for a cross-platform system that reduced reliance on disconnected spreadsheets and gave teams clearer visibility across fleet availability, reporting and service payment workflows.

The problem

Three teams managing train performance across disconnected spreadsheets. Controllers worked from hours-old data. Maintenance logs got lost in handovers. Finance reconciled mismatched records after the fact.

"We're making decisions about the fleet based on yesterday's data. By the time the spreadsheet gets updated, the situation has already changed."

, Operations controller, synthesised from stakeholder sessions
Key design decisions
01. One system, two completely different contexts

Maintenance staff in depots needed to log a fault fast, one hand free, a categorically different context from an operations manager analysing fleet trends. Mobile was designed around the smallest unit of work; desktop around density and insight.

02. Information hierarchy across 13+ screen types

Status before detail, exceptions before routine, actions before information. Operations sees live status. Management sees trends. Finance sees payment-relevant data. Same source, different lens.

Outcomes
3
User groups aligned
13+
Screen types designed
Web + mobile
Cross-platform workflows
Reflection

Working as the sole designer on this project taught me to write the why before the what and take full ownership of the design process.

Case study 03
Insurance Management App
Startup · UX Designer, Design Team · Mobile-first Web + Android · 2022
InsuranceFintechMobile App DesignOnboardingAndroid + Web
Opening

This insurance app was designed for a founder-led startup exploring a simpler way for customers to manage policies, insured objects, payments, support requests and document signing. My focus was the mobile-first onboarding and document-signing experience, the point where users decide whether the product feels trustworthy enough to continue.

The problem

Insurance users often need to share sensitive personal, financial and policy information before they fully trust the product. The experience needed to explain why information was required, reduce uncertainty around document signing, and make complex policy tasks feel clear on a small screen.

"I don’t understand what I’m signing. I just click through and hope for the best."

, Insurance app user, representative sentiment
Design tools

Figma and Adobe XD were used for flows, wireframes, interactive prototypes and high-fidelity mobile screens. Photoshop and Illustrator supported visual polish, image preparation, icon refinement and presentation-ready design assets.

Key design decisions
01. Two-phase registration

Phase 1 framed around access. Phase 2 framed around value. Users who completed Phase 1 were already invested; the second phase followed naturally. Existing data pre-filled wherever possible.

02. Document signing, transparent not bureaucratic

Plain-language explanation before every signature. Drawn signatures for formal legal documents, toggle for lower-stakes confirmations. A user who signs because they understand, not because they gave up.

03. Mobile-first patterns, then web scale-up

The mobile experience carried the most sensitive tasks: onboarding, verification, document review, signing and support. Web screens scaled the same system into denser contract-management views without changing the core interaction logic.

Outcomes
4
Core mobile journeys
2-phase
Onboarding structure
System
Reusable mobile patterns

Android app screens across the four main product flows: dashboard, account creation, contract management, and services. Designed for one-handed use with a consistent component system throughout.

Reflection

The strongest design decision was slowing users down at the right moments. For this product, trust mattered more than speed alone. The experience needed to help people understand what they were doing before asking them to continue.

How I work

My design process

01
Start with people

Before any wireframe, I need to understand who is using the system, under what conditions, and what is genuinely hard for them. Research informs every decision.

02
Design with reasoning

Every design decision needs a clear reason. I explore alternatives, test the logic, consider accessibility and technical constraints, then refine the pattern until it works.

03
Test and iterate

Assumptions get challenged early. Usability testing or stakeholder review , I would rather find the friction in a prototype than in a live system.

04
Measure outcomes

Design is only as good as the outcome it produces. I connect decisions to results, for users and the business, not just deliverables.
